evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on case studies from four cities in the global South (Guarulhos, Arequipa, Lima and Durban), this article analyzes recent changes in these configurations, with particular attention to the role and power of the municipality in this process. This paper explores to what extent these new configurations reveal a move towards resilience, transition or even transformation.

What are the main consequences of recent changes in the institutional framework and rescaling of responsibilities for urban water governance, with specific attention to the mandates and roles of municipalities?
To what extent do the new institutional structures and responsibilities foster social learning and knowledge generation in water governance?

The full breadth of the reforms and the dynamics these have created in the different cities and basins are treated in more detail in four accompanying papers, which will be published in Environment and Urbanization Vol 26, No 2 (October 2014). They all draw on the analytical framework presented in this paper.

All three countries have experienced a significant change in water governance structures either after a return to democracy (Brazil and Peru) or the establishment of democracy (South Africa), which resulted in a decentralization of mandates and responsibilities in water governance and management and an increased emphasis on participation.

There are signs of transition, or even transformation, in water governance, but water management decisions are still based on classic sectoral and economic interests and knowledge, maintaining the status quo.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access as its object of analysis. Although the paper covers municipal governance of urban drinking water and sanitation alongside river-basin resource management—and notes city-level network coverage in Table 3 as background context plus secondary summary remarks on Durban's free basic water and peripheral sanitation—its inquiry focuses on institutional governance configurations, municipal mandates, and social learning.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it examines legal, institutional, and governance reforms (Brazil's 1997 Water Law, Peru's 2009 Law on Water Resources, South Africa's 1997 Water Services Act and 1998 National Water Act, decentralization to municipalities, and river basin councils). However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification (narrow = no) because it analyzes macro-governance rescaling, river-basin participation, and multi-actor social learning for climate adaptation rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (brief mentions of utility ownership/control and Durban's indigent free basic water allocation appear only as descriptive case background). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: Unclear in this standalone text: the paper draws on four city case studies from the EU FP7 Chance2Sustain research programme and briefly refers to fieldwork reports and 'respondents' (p. 13), but presents no methods section, sampling frame, data-collection procedures, or primary data analysis, explicitly serving as an analytical framework and comparative overview for four forthcoming companion articles (note 6).
criterion_notes.c4: No service-access outcome is evaluated. The paper's three research questions and comparative findings assess (1) municipal mandates, power, and autonomy in urban/basin water governance, (2) social learning and knowledge co-production among institutional actors, and (3) whether governance shifts reflect Pelling's categories of resilience, transition, or transformation—not household or community access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5 (and Criterion 7): the unit of analysis is the city/basin governance system, no empirical data-collection or analytical study design is reported in the article, and no household- or community-level service-access exposure-outcome relationship is identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, an eligible review language without translation.

study_design: Comparative case-study overview / analytical framework paper (empirical methods not reported in article)
population_and_sample: Four southern cities / metropolitan water governance systems: Guarulhos (Brazil), Metropolitan Lima and Arequipa (Peru), and Durban / eThekwini Municipality (South Africa); specific empirical sample and respondent counts not reported
exposure: Changes in national water laws, decentralization / rescaling of water governance responsibilities to river basin councils and municipalities, and participatory / multi-actor governance arrangements
outcome: Municipal mandates and autonomy in water governance, social learning and knowledge generation among governance actors, and mode of adaptation (resilience, transition, or transformation)
rationale: Excluded at full text (E04: Wrong outcome). This article introduces an analytical framework (based on Pelling's resilience, transition, and transformation typology) and provides a high-level comparative overview of water governance reforms across four cities (Guarulhos, Lima, Arequipa, and Durban) ahead of four forthcoming companion case-study papers. Its evaluated outcomes are municipal mandates/autonomy in urban and river-basin governance, institutional social learning and knowledge co-production, and regime adaptation modes (resilience, transition, or transformation), rather than household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes (city connection rates in Table 3 and brief secondary remarks on Durban's free basic water and peripheral sanitation serve only as background context). It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it examines macro-governance rescaling and multi-actor participation rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access, and it reports no empirical data-collection methods or sample details in this publication. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the decision remains exclude due to the lack of a service-access outcome and identifiable empirical design.
